luna.caption: Workflow diagram of generating, evaluating, and learning from alternative self-edits to a language model.
luna.description: A process diagram shows a starting context (Ctx, in a blue box) entering a language model with parameters θ_t. The model branches into three candidate self-edits, SE₁, SE₂, and SE₃. Each candidate points to an Optimize step with its loss, 𝓛(SEᵢ, θ_t), and then to a corresponding updated parameter set, θ′ᵢ. To the right of a vertical divider, each candidate is tested: a “Test” input and blue input block feed a language model with θ′ᵢ, which produces an answer (Ans) in a blue box. The first and second answers have check marks; the third has a cross. A curly brace groups these evaluation outcomes. The RL Data box shows a tuple containing the state (Ctx and θ_t), action (SE), and reward (✓/✗). The grouped rewards and RL data are associated with a Policy Update that produces θ_{t+1}.

luna.caption: Line chart comparing accuracy for four skill methods across four language models; WikiSkill is highest at every model size.
luna.description: A line chart with Accuracy (%) on the vertical axis, marked at 30%, 45%, 60%, and 75%, and four model categories on the horizontal axis: Qwen3.5-4B, Qwen3.5-9B, Qwen3.6-27B, and Gemini 3.5 Flash. The legend identifies No skill as blue circles, EvoSkill as green squares, SkillOpt as orange triangles, and WikiSkill as yellow diamonds. Estimated accuracy rises across the models for all four methods. WikiSkill leads at each category and its advantage is larger for the stronger models. No skill is lowest at each category. EvoSkill and SkillOpt are close: EvoSkill is slightly lower than SkillOpt at Qwen3.5-4B, then slightly higher at Qwen3.5-9B and Qwen3.6-27B; they finish at about the same level for Gemini 3.5 Flash.

luna.caption: A four-stage WikiSkill workflow links three knowledge layers through trace analysis, skill updates, validation, and iterative feedback.
luna.description: A flow diagram has three wide, rounded gray layers stacked above a row of four colored process boxes. From top to bottom: the Skill Layer (skills/) contains “Evolving Procedural Knowledge” and is marked “Reversible, Conditional Update”; a folder icon represents the stored skills. The Wiki Layer (wiki/) contains “Structured Patterns & Evolution Logs” and is marked “Compounding, Never Reset”; a lit-bulb-and-books icon represents organized knowledge. The Raw Layer (raw/) contains “Immutable Execution Traces” and is marked “Permanent, Write Once”; a lock icon represents protected, immutable traces. The four stages run left to right: Step 1, “Inference Agent,” executes rollouts on the Training Set; a robot icon represents the agent. Step 2, “Wiki Maintainer,” performs root-cause analysis on traces; a tool/gears icon represents maintenance and analysis. Step 3, “Skill Proposer,” proposes skill updates from Wiki and Traces; a lit bulb represents proposing ideas. Step 4, “Gating & Rollback,” evaluates the skill candidate on the Validation Set; its icon shows a checked box and an X, representing the gate’s accept/reject or rollback decisions. Horizontal arrows connect Step 1 to Step 2 (blue), Step 2 to Step 3 (red), and Step 3 to Step 4 (yellow). Between the layers and the stages, a blue arrow labeled “Inject Skills” points down into Step 1, while a blue arrow labeled “Write Traces” points up from Step 1 to the Raw Layer. A red arrow labeled “Sample Traces” points down from the Raw Layer to Step 2, and a red arrow labeled “Consolidate Patterns” points up from Step 2 to the Wiki Layer. Three yellow arrows point down into Step 3 from the Skill, Wiki, and Raw layers; their label is “Read Skill, Wiki, Traces.” From Step 4, a green upward arrow labeled “Update the Skill if Better” leads to the Skill Layer, and another green upward arrow labeled “Update Wiki Logs” leads to the Wiki Layer. A green return path labeled “Next Iteration” runs from Step 4 beneath the stages and points upward into Step 1. Short unlabeled blue vertical connector segments also appear between the stacked layers at the left.

luna.caption: Diagram of how persistent Wiki records and observed patterns inform the creation and refinement of an active skill.
luna.description: A two-column process diagram. The left column is headed “Persistent Wiki Layer (wiki/)” with a lightbulb-over-books icon, and the right is “Active Skill Layer (skills/)” with a folder icon. In the Wiki column, the top box, “skill-impact.md,” records a diff for Iteration 0: creating “goal-directed-action” is marked REJECTED; the diff shows “-/dev/null,” “+ goal-directed-action/SKILL.md,” “+ # Goal-Directed Action,” and an ellipsis. Iteration 1 creation of “break-repetition-loop” and Iteration 4 update of it are both marked ACCEPTED. Below, “logs.md” records Iteration 0 creation of take-examine-move-loop.md (train: 00, 02) and rejection of skill “goal-directed-action” (val score = 0.72); Iteration 1 records errors re-occurring (train: 01, 02), “Use-Examine Loop (NEW)” in train: 30, 31, fresh evidence appended to take-examine-move-loop.md, and acceptance of skill “break-repetition-loop” (val score = 0.78). The lower “patterns” box contains take-examine-move-loop.md, describing an agent taking an item, examining it, putting it back, and repeating; its evidence lists Iteration 0 train 00, 02; Iteration 1 train 01; and Iterations 2–4 train 02 persisting, with 00/01 showing recovery from loops. It also contains multi-operation-loop.md, describing cycles of actions on the same item without checking completion; evidence lists Iteration 2 train 22, 24 and Iterations 3–4 train 24 persisting. In the Active Skill column, a green container titled “break-repetition-loop” holds PURPOSE.md and SKILL.md. PURPOSE.md says the skill was created as break-repetition-loop; the previous goal-directed-action attempt was rejected for being too abstract, and this version is more concise and uses concrete action patterns. SKILL.md says to apply the skill whenever the agent is about to repeat an action. Its first rule, “Never Return an Item to Its Origin Location,” contrasts a failing example (take clock from desk → examine → move clock to desk) with a successful one (take clock → go to shelf → move clock to shelf). A second rule says agents that take items and perform operations often get stuck repeating the same operation, and prescribes each operation type once per item. An anti-pattern is “Take → Operate → Move → Take (INFINITE CYCLE)”; the fix is to complete take → operate → move once and not repeat. A separate “other-skill” bar with an ellipsis appears below the container. Colored arrows connect the Wiki records to the active skill: a red arrow from the rejected Iteration 0 proposal to PURPOSE.md is labeled “Prior Rejection History Explains Skill Rationale”; green arrows from the accepted Iteration 1 and Iteration 4 entries to SKILL.md are labeled “Accepted Proposed Skill Update”; a blue arrow from patterns toward logs.md is labeled “Evolution Log Chronologically Records Patterns and Decisions”; and orange arrows from patterns toward rules in SKILL.md are labeled “Documented Patterns Motivate the Skill Update Proposals at Iterations 1 and 4.”

luna.caption: Two stacked bar charts comparing Answer Agent scores before reinforcement learning and after PPO or GRPO.
luna.description: A pair of stacked bar charts, each with a vertical axis labeled “Score in %” and categories F1, B1, and J. The legend identifies blue as Before RL, red as PPO, and green as GRPO. In each bar, the colored segments stack upward in that order. The values listed below are estimated readings at the top edge of each segment, so later series’ readings are cumulative totals, not the individual segment heights. In the Llama3.1-8B-Instruct chart, the estimated cumulative tops for Before RL / PPO / GRPO are: F1 about 27 / 34 / 37%, B1 about 20 / 28 / 31%, and J about 48 / 49 / 53%. In the GPT-4o-mini chart, they are: F1 about 31 / 46 / 51%, B1 about 25 / 37 / 43%, and J about 56 / 65 / 72%. J is the highest-scoring category in both charts; the GPT-4o-mini bars are higher than the corresponding Llama3.1-8B-Instruct bars in all three categories. Both charts show PPO and GRPO adding to the Before RL scores, with the largest overall totals for J.

luna.caption: Two-panel line chart comparing PPO and GRPO training rewards for two language models.
luna.description: Two side-by-side line charts show training reward over horizontal-axis values from 0 to 200. The left panel, “(a) Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct,” and the right panel, “(b) Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct,” each plot PPO as a red line and GRPO as a blue line, as identified by the legends. The vertical axis is Training Reward; the left panel shows ticks at 0.0, 0.1, 0.2, and 0.3, with the plotted scale extending to about 0.4. Both series are noisy. In the Llama panel, GRPO rises more quickly at first and is generally ahead early on, while PPO catches up and ends slightly higher; both finish at broadly similar rewards. In the Qwen panel, GRPO also rises earlier, and the lines then remain close, ending at similar levels with GRPO slightly higher. The horizontal axis has numeric ticks but no visible axis title. Values in chart_values are estimated read-offs at the labeled horizontal-axis ticks; no point values are printed.

luna.caption: Three-panel scatter chart comparing latency and accuracy for three inference pipelines.
luna.description: The target is a three-panel scatter chart. Each panel plots Accuracy (%) vertically against Latency (s) horizontally on a logarithmic scale, with ticks including 10⁰, 10¹, and 10². The panels are F1 (↑), B1 (↑), and J (↑). The legend identifies Base in blue, Base + Reranker in orange, and Memory-R1 (GRPO) in green; circles denote p50 and triangles denote p95. Approximate read-offs show that Memory-R1 has the highest accuracy and lowest latency in all three panels: about 45.5% F1, 37.7% B1, and 62.3% J, with its p50 and p95 marks close together at low latency. Base has the lowest accuracy—about 30.5% F1, 22.3% B1, and 45.8% J—and its p95 latency is much higher than its p50. Base + Reranker is intermediate in F1 and B1 (about 32.5% and 24.7%) and reaches about 60% J; its latency marks are also well to the right of Memory-R1’s. Values below are estimated from plotted positions; latency x-coordinates are approximate read-offs in seconds.

luna.caption: A rollout workflow turns success and failure traces into patches that are merged into an evolved skill.
luna.description:
A left-to-right process diagram begins with a purple skill-like symbol beside crossed tools, labeled “Rollout Using Skills.” An arrow leads to a dashed rounded box labeled “Traces,” containing three rows. The green “Success Trace” says “Agent successfully matched rows across two sheets.” It carries a magenta T+ mark and a green circled check. The first red “Error Trace” says “MEDIAN(IF(xxx))” returned None in recalc.py; it carries a magenta T− mark and a red circled X. The second red “Error Trace” says “recalc.py” can’t handle excel array formulas; it also carries T− and a red circled X. Each row has a right-pointing arrow to a purple symbol marked in magenta A+ for the success row and A− for each error row, then another right-pointing arrow to its corresponding patch card.

A dashed rounded area titled “Patches” contains three cards. The green first card has an “Addition” icon and the heading “Patch1: add new pattern from success trace.” Its bullets read “Cast ID columns to str”; “Cast numeric columns to float before”; and “Cross-sheet row matching to prevent silent type-mismatch failures.” The red second card has an “Addition” icon and the heading “Patch2: add new warning from error trace.” Its bullets say “Array formulas silently fail in LibreOffice” and “Pre-calculate in Python and write the result as a literal value instead.” The red-bordered third card has an “Edition” icon and the heading “Patch3: Deepening existing rules from error trace.” Its bullets say “Use formulas, not hardcoded values.”; “Same rule, now with explicit text-function”; and “Add warning against auto-applying .strip”.

The first patch’s output line runs right and then down toward the merge; the second patch connects directly rightward; and the third patch’s output runs right and then up. All three feed into a purple merge symbol labeled “Merge Patches.” A right-pointing arrow leads from it to a crossed-tools symbol with a crown, labeled “Evolved Skill.”

luna.caption: Two-panel chart comparing success rates across parallel and sequential scaling factors for three MaTTS configurations.
luna.description: A two-panel line-and-bar chart plots Success Rate (SR) against scaling factor k = 1–5. Both y-axes run from 36 to 56, with ticks every 4 units. In each panel, gray bars show “MaTTS w/o memory,” blue dotted lines with diamond markers show “MaTTS w/o aggregation,” and solid blue lines with circular markers show “MaTTS.” The values are printed next to the marks. In Parallel Scaling, the gray bars rise from 39.0 at k=1 to 42.2 at k=5; the no-aggregation line is 49.7, 49.7, 51.3, 52.9, and 52.4, rising through k=4 then dipping; the MaTTS line is 49.7, 50.3, 52.4, 54.0, and 55.1, increasing throughout and finishing highest. The two line series coincide at 49.7 at k=1. In Sequential Scaling, the gray bars are 39.0, 37.4, 38.5, 40.1, and 40.6, dipping at k=2 before rising; the no-aggregation line is 49.7, 50.8, 51.9, 52.4, and 51.9, peaking at k=4; the MaTTS line is 49.7, 51.9, 53.5, 54.0, and 54.5, increasing throughout and finishing highest. The line series coincide at 49.7 at k=1. In both panels, the MaTTS line is at or above the no-aggregation line, while the gray bars are lower than both line series.

luna.caption: Success rates for three scaling settings across four memory methods.
luna.description: Grouped bar chart with a gray dashed line and circular markers. The vertical axis is Success Rate (SR), ranging from 35 to 60 with ticks every 5. The horizontal categories are No Memory, Synapse, AWM, and ReasoningBank. Pink bars represent Pass@1, blue bars represent Best-of-5, and the gray dashed line represents No Scaling. Printed values are: No Memory—Pass@1 39.0, Best-of-5 42.2, No Scaling 39.0; Synapse—41.2, 44.4, 40.6; AWM—45.5, 47.6, 44.4; ReasoningBank—53.0, 55.1, 49.7, respectively. Best-of-5 is higher than Pass@1 in every category, and both scaling results rise across the categories; ReasoningBank has the highest values for all three series.
